prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a valuation came in low. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a valuation comes in below the purchase price or expected balance, I check whether the shortfall is driven by market evidence, property condition, or a mismatch in comparables before I ask for anything else. That usually tells me whether the case needs re-pricing, extra deposit, or a fresh review of the report."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the loan-to-value would move into a higher band because of a low valuation, I recalculate the affordability and product fit straight away. A small shift in value can change the decision more than the income side does."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the valuation is low on a remortgage, I look first for signs of deferred maintenance or features the valuer has marked down, because those cases often need a practical property discussion rather than a credit one. It saves time if I separate property risk from borrower risk early."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the valuation is borderline, I prefer to compare it against recent local evidence and the valuer’s commentary rather than challenge the figure on gut feel. A clear, evidence-led query is more likely to get a useful answer than a broad objection."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the borrower has enough savings or equity to bridge a modest valuation shortfall, I treat the case as potentially recoverable if the rest of the file is strong. That makes it worth checking whether they can adjust the deposit, reduce the loan, or accept a smaller advance."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the valuation is low because the property is unusual, I ask whether the marketability issue is temporary or structural. If the concern is permanent, I expect the risk to remain even if the borrower is otherwise well qualified."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a low valuation follows a rapid market change, I look at whether the offer assumptions are simply out of date.
